marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q015.takeaway: The head of the talus is the keystone at the summit of the medial longitudinal arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q015.displayText:
The head of the talus is the keystone at the summit of the medial longitudinal arch.

The keystone (summit) of the medial longitudinal arch is formed by the talus.
emphasis: The head of the talus is the keystone at the summit of the medial longitudinal arch

rationales.b: The cuboid is associated with the lateral arch, not the summit of the medial arch.
rationales.c: The calcaneus forms the posterior pillar, not the keystone.
rationales.d: Navicular supports the talar head but is not the keystone itself.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q016.takeaway: Peroneus longus supports the lateral and transverse arches; it is not a principal support of the medial longitudinal arch.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q016.displayText:
Peroneus longus supports the lateral and transverse arches; it is not a principal support of the medial longitudinal arch.

Peroneus longus maintains the lateral longitudinal arch and not the medial arch.

The muscles, tendons and aponeurosis maintaining the longitudinal arches act as slings, suspending the arches from above, and as tie beams (bowstrings) between anterior and posterior pillars that prevent separation of the pillars.
emphasis: Peroneus longus supports the lateral and transverse arches; it is not a principal support of the medial longitudinal arch

rationales.b: Tibialis posterior is a major dynamic support of the medial arch; dysfunction can flatten it.
rationales.c: Flexor digitorum longus helps support the medial arch through its plantar course.
rationales.d: The plantar aponeurosis is a passive tie that supports the longitudinal arch.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q017.takeaway: Tibialis posterior passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, not beneath the superior extensor retinaculum.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q017.displayText:
Tibialis posterior passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, not beneath the superior extensor retinaculum.

The tendon of tibialis posterior does not pass deep to the superior extensor retinaculum of the foot.

Structures passing deep to the superior and inferior extensor retinacula include tibialis anterior tendon, extensor hallucis longus tendon, deep peroneal nerve, extensor digitorum longus tendon and peroneus tertius tendon. The anterior tibial vessels pass deep to the superior retinaculum and continue as dorsalis pedis deep to the inferior retinaculum.

The tendon of tibialis posterior passes deep to the flexor retinaculum.
emphasis: Tibialis posterior passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, not beneath the superior extensor retinaculum

rationales.a: The deep fibular (peroneal) nerve runs under the extensor retinacula on the anterior ankle.
rationales.b: Peroneus tertius crosses anterior to the ankle beneath the extensor retinacula.
rationales.d: Extensor digitorum longus tendons pass anteriorly under the extensor retinacula.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q018.takeaway: The superior band of the inferior extensor retinaculum attaches medially to the medial malleolus, not the fibula.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q018.displayText:
The superior band of the inferior extensor retinaculum attaches medially to the medial malleolus, not the fibula.

The upper band is attached to the medial malleolus of the tibia and not to the fibula.

The inferior extensor retinaculum is a Y-shaped band lying anterior to the ankle joint. The stem of the Y is at the lateral end attached to the upper surface of calcaneus; the limbs lie medially, with the proximal limb attaching to the medial malleolus and the distal limb blending with the plantar aponeurosis.

Structures passing deep include peroneus tertius, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, tibialis anterior, anterior tibial vessels/dorsalis pedis, and deep peroneal nerve.
emphasis: The superior band of the inferior extensor retinaculum attaches medially to the medial malleolus, not the fibula

rationales.b: The inferior extensor retinaculum is characteristically Y-shaped.
rationales.c: The inferior band blends with deep fascia on the sole side of the foot.
rationales.d: The retinaculum is anchored laterally to the calcaneus.

marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q019.takeaway: From medial to lateral behind the medial malleolus, the first flexor-retinaculum canal contains tibialis posterior tendon.
marrow__ANAT_CH58_Q019.displayText:
From medial to lateral behind the medial malleolus, the first flexor-retinaculum canal contains tibialis posterior tendon.

Tibialis posterior tendon is the most medial structure passing through the canals in the flexor retinaculum of the foot.

The flexor retinaculum converts grooves on the tibia and calcaneus into canals. From medial to lateral the structures are: tibialis posterior tendon, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial vessels, tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus tendon.
emphasis: From medial to lateral behind the medial malleolus, the first flexor-retinaculum canal contains tibialis posterior tendon

rationales.a: Flexor digitorum longus is lateral to tibialis posterior in the tarsal-tunnel order.
rationales.b: The tibial nerve lies farther lateral than the two medial flexor tendons.
rationales.d: Posterior tibial vessels also lie lateral to the tendons in the tunnel.
